Hands-on Ex06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Delineating ICT regions across the townships of Shan State, Myanmar

Author

Meng Tingyu

Published

October 2, 2026

Modified

October 2, 2026

What this exercise is about

This exercise groups the 55 townships of Shan State in Myanmar into regions with similar access to information and communication technology. The grouping uses six household ICT measures from the 2014 census, radio, television, land line phone, mobile phone, computer and internet at home.

Planners often want regions that are both homogeneous and joined together on the map. Ordinary cluster analysis only looks at the first condition. The second half of the exercise adds the map back in, first with SKATER, which cuts a minimum spanning tree of neighbouring townships, and then with ClustGeo, which lets me choose how much weight geography gets.

The work is split into six parts. Part 1 explores the variables with charts and choropleth maps, Part 2 checks correlations, and Part 3 runs hierarchical clustering. Part 4 and Part 5 cover the two spatially constrained methods, and Part 6 profiles the clusters.

Setting up

The data

Two datasets come from the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU).

The first is myanmar_township_boundaries, an ESRI shapefile with the polygon boundary of every township in Myanmar. The second is Shan-ICT.csv, an extract of the 2014 Myanmar Population and Housing Census at township level. It has the number of households in each township and the number that own each of the six ICT items.

I put the shapefile in data/geospatial and the csv in data/aspatial, and added an empty data/rds folder for the intermediate files. The notes use chap12/data/..., and I changed every path to match this folder layout.

Packages

Show the code 
pacman::p_load(spdep, tmap, sf, ClustGeo, 
               ggpubr, cluster, factoextra, NbClust,
               heatmaply, corrplot, psych, tidyverse, GGally)

The packages fall into five groups. sf and spdep handle the spatial data, and tidyverse covers readr, dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2 for the attribute data. tmap draws the choropleth maps. corrplot, ggpubr, heatmaply, psych and GGally are used to visualise the variables, and cluster, factoextra, NbClust and ClustGeo run the cluster analysis.

Notergdal is no longer needed

The package list in the notes mentions rgdal. It was retired from CRAN in 2023, and sf now does all of its reading and writing work, so I left it out. The p_load() call in the notes already does not include it.

Importing the township boundaries

st_read() reads the whole country. I keep only the three parts of Shan State and the six columns from state name to township code.

shan_sf <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", 
                   layer = "myanmar_township_boundaries") %>%
  filter(ST %in% c("Shan (East)", "Shan (North)", "Shan (South)")) %>%
  select(c(2:7))

Deriving penetration rates

The raw counts mostly measure how big a township is. A township with many households will also have many households with a radio, and that says nothing about how common radios are there. I divided each count by the total number of households and multiplied by 1,000 to get the number of owning households per thousand.

Show the code 
ict_derived <- ict %>%
  mutate(`RADIO_PR` = `Radio`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`TV_PR` = `Television`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`LLPHONE_PR` = `Land line phone`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`MPHONE_PR` = `Mobile phone`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`COMPUTER_PR` = `Computer`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`INTERNET_PR` = `Internet at home`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  rename(`DT_PCODE` =`District Pcode`,`DT`=`District Name`,
         `TS_PCODE`=`Township Pcode`, `TS`=`Township Name`,
         `TT_HOUSEHOLDS`=`Total households`,
         `RADIO`=`Radio`, `TV`=`Television`, 
         `LLPHONE`=`Land line phone`, `MPHONE`=`Mobile phone`,
         `COMPUTER`=`Computer`, `INTERNET`=`Internet at home`)

Six new fields now sit at the end of the table, RADIO_PR, TV_PR, LLPHONE_PR, MPHONE_PR, COMPUTER_PR and INTERNET_PR. Television is the most common item, with a median of 517 households per thousand. Computers and home internet are rare, with medians of 19 and 23 per thousand.

Part 1, Exploratory data analysis

Distribution of radio ownership

A histogram shows the overall shape of a variable, and a boxplot picks out outliers. I started with the raw count of households with a radio.

Show the code 
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")
Show the code 
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color="black", 
               fill="light blue")

The count is heavily right skewed, with a skewness of about 2.6. Three quarters of the townships have fewer than 6,200 radio households, and three outliers sit far to the right, Taunggyi with 30,176, Lashio with 15,307 and Nyaungshwe with 13,801. These are also among the four townships with the most households.

Next I plotted the radio penetration rate.

Show the code 
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")
Show the code 
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color="black", 
               fill="light blue")

The course asks what the two distributions reveal. Dividing by households removes most of the skew. RADIO_PR has a mean of 216 and a median of 211 per thousand, and its skewness drops to 0.48. The boxplot now flags only one outlier, Ywangan, where 485 of every thousand households own a radio. Taunggyi, the largest outlier in the raw counts, has a rate of 365 and sits inside the whiskers, so its earlier position came from size alone.

Distributions of all six rates

I drew one histogram for each rate and arranged them with ggarrange() from ggpubr.

Show the code 
radio <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

tv <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `TV_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

llphone <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `LLPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

mphone <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `MPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

computer <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `COMPUTER_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

internet <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `INTERNET_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")
Show the code 
ggarrange(radio, tv, llphone, mphone, computer, internet, 
          ncol = 3, 
          nrow = 2)

The six rates fall into two shapes. Radio, television and mobile phone are roughly bell shaped, with television slightly skewed to the left (skewness -0.38). Land line phone, computer and internet are right skewed, with skewness between 1.3 and 1.8, because most townships have very low rates and a handful have much higher ones.

Joining the census data to the boundaries

The choropleth maps need the rates attached to the polygons. left_join() keeps shan_sf as the base, so the result is still an sf object, and adds the columns of ict_derived by matching TS_PCODE.

Show the code 
shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf, 
                     ict_derived, by=c("TS_PCODE"="TS_PCODE"))
  
write_rds(shan_sf, "data/rds/shan_sf.rds")

All 55 township codes match in both directions, so no township is dropped or left without data.

NoteWhy TS.x and TS.y appear

The notes mention a message naming the join field. With by written out there is no message. Both tables have DT, DT_PCODE and TS columns besides the key, so dplyr keeps both copies and adds the suffixes .x and .y. I checked that TS.x and TS.y hold the same township name in all 55 rows. That is why the later code refers to TS.x.

Show the code 
shan_sf <- read_rds("data/rds/shan_sf.rds")

Choropleth map of the radio penetration rate

qtm() gives a quick map with default settings.

Show the code 
qtm(shan_sf, "RADIO_PR")

Radio ownership is highest in the west of Shan South and Shan North. Ywangan, Pindaya and Lawksawk near Taunggyi and Mabein in the north west all exceed 380 per thousand. The lowest rates are in the north east along the Chinese border, Konkyan and Laukkaing in the Kokang area at 21 and 53, and Narphan and Pangwaun in the Wa area at about 75.

Counts versus rates on the map

To show how much the counts depend on township size, I mapped total households next to the number of radio households. The notes use tmap v3 syntax here, and I translated it to v4, where the classification goes into tm_scale_intervals().

Show the code 
TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Total households")) + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

RADIO.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "RADIO",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Number Radio")) + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO.map,
             asp=NA, ncol=2)

The two maps look almost the same. Taunggyi and Lashio are in the top class on both, and the correlation between total households and radio households across the 55 townships is 0.94.

Next I put total households next to the rate. The notes do this with two variables in one tm_polygons() call and tm_facets(sync = TRUE). In v4, a vector of variables in fill already produces facets, and fill.free = TRUE gives each one its own Jenks classes.

Show the code 
tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks"),
              fill.free = TRUE,
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_facets(ncol = 2) +
  tm_layout(outer.margins = 0, asp = 0)
WarningTranslating the tmap v3 code

Three changes were needed for tmap 4.4. tm_fill(col = ..., n = 5, style = "jenks", title = ...) became tm_polygons(fill = ..., fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = ...)). tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) became tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5), since a border is a line. tm_legend(legend.position = ...) was replaced by a position inside the fill.legend argument.

The course asks whether I can see the differences. The rate map breaks the link with size. Taunggyi, the largest township, drops to the fourth of five classes for RADIO_PR, and Lashio, the second largest, falls to the middle class at 236 per thousand. Small townships such as Mabein (8,632 households) and Monghpyak (6,165) move into the top class. The correlation between total households and RADIO_PR is only 0.34, which confirms that the rate measures something different from size.

Part 2, Correlation analysis

Cluster analysis treats each variable as a separate dimension. Two variables that carry almost the same information would count that information twice, so I checked the correlations between the six rates first.

Show the code 
cluster_vars.cor = cor(ict_derived[,12:17])
corrplot.mixed(cluster_vars.cor,
         lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")

COMPUTER_PR and INTERNET_PR have the strongest correlation, 0.87, so I keep only one of them. Following the notes, I keep COMPUTER_PR. The next highest pairs are MPHONE_PR with COMPUTER_PR at 0.74 and TV_PR with MPHONE_PR at 0.72. They are high but well below 0.87, and the notes keep all of them.

Radio stands apart from the rest. Its correlation with the other rates ranges from -0.31 with land line phones to 0.24 with television. Radio is common in townships where the more modern items are rare, so it adds information the other variables do not have.

Part 3, Hierarchical cluster analysis

Extracting the clustering variables

I dropped the geometry and kept the township name with the five clustering variables.

cluster_vars <- shan_sf %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL) %>%
  select("TS.x", "RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR")

NoteSaving shan_ict before reading it back

The notes read shan_ict.rds at this point but never write it. I added the write_rds() so the file exists before read_rds() loads it.

Show the code 
write_rds(shan_ict, "data/rds/shan_ict.rds")
shan_ict <- read_rds("data/rds/shan_ict.rds")

Data standardisation

The five variables have very different ranges. Mobile phones run from 36 to 735 per thousand, and computers from 3 to 92. Without standardisation, a variable with a large range has more pull on the distances between townships. The notes show two ways to standardise.

Min-max standardisation

normalize() from heatmaply rescales each variable to run from 0 to 1.

Show the code 
shan_ict.std <- normalize(shan_ict)
summary(shan_ict.std)
    RADIO_PR          TV_PR          LLPHONE_PR       MPHONE_PR     
 Min.   :0.0000   Min.   :0.0000   Min.   :0.0000   Min.   :0.0000  
 1st Qu.:0.2544   1st Qu.:0.4600   1st Qu.:0.1123   1st Qu.:0.2199  
 Median :0.4097   Median :0.5523   Median :0.1948   Median :0.3846  
 Mean   :0.4199   Mean   :0.5416   Mean   :0.2703   Mean   :0.3972  
 3rd Qu.:0.5330   3rd Qu.:0.6750   3rd Qu.:0.3746   3rd Qu.:0.5608  
 Max.   :1.0000   Max.   :1.0000   Max.   :1.0000   Max.   :1.0000  
  COMPUTER_PR     
 Min.   :0.00000  
 1st Qu.:0.09598  
 Median :0.17607  
 Mean   :0.23692  
 3rd Qu.:0.29868  
 Max.   :1.00000

Every variable now has a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 1. The means differ, from 0.24 for COMPUTER_PR to 0.54 for TV_PR, because the shape of each distribution is kept.

Z-score standardisation

scale() subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. I used describe() from psych instead of summary() because it reports the standard deviation as well.

Show the code 
shan_ict.z <- scale(shan_ict)
describe(shan_ict.z)
            vars  n mean sd median trimmed  mad   min  max range  skew kurtosis
RADIO_PR       1 55    0  1  -0.04   -0.06 0.94 -1.85 2.55  4.40  0.48    -0.27
TV_PR          2 55    0  1   0.05    0.04 0.78 -2.47 2.09  4.56 -0.38    -0.23
LLPHONE_PR     3 55    0  1  -0.33   -0.15 0.68 -1.19 3.20  4.39  1.37     1.49
MPHONE_PR      4 55    0  1  -0.05   -0.06 1.01 -1.58 2.40  3.98  0.48    -0.34
COMPUTER_PR    5 55    0  1  -0.26   -0.18 0.64 -1.03 3.31  4.34  1.80     2.96
              se
RADIO_PR    0.13
TV_PR       0.13
LLPHONE_PR  0.13
MPHONE_PR   0.13
COMPUTER_PR 0.13

All five variables now have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. The skewness values are the same as before standardisation, 1.80 for COMPUTER_PR and 1.37 for LLPHONE_PR.

TipWhen to use z-scores

The notes warn that z-scores should only be used if the variables can be assumed to come from a normal distribution. COMPUTER_PR and LLPHONE_PR are clearly skewed, so a z-score of 3 means something different for them than for TV_PR. Min-max scaling makes no such assumption, but a single extreme value squeezes everyone else into a narrow part of the 0 to 1 range.

Visualising the standardised variables

I compared the histogram of RADIO_PR before standardisation and after each method.

Show the code 
r <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue") +
  ggtitle("Raw values without standardisation")

shan_ict_s_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.std)
s <- ggplot(data=shan_ict_s_df, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue") +
  ggtitle("Min-Max Standardisation")

shan_ict_z_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.z)
z <- ggplot(data=shan_ict_z_df, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue") +
  ggtitle("Z-score Standardisation")

ggarrange(r, s, z,
          ncol = 3,
          nrow = 1)
Show the code 
r <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_density(color="black",
               fill="light blue") +
  ggtitle("Raw values without standardisation")

shan_ict_s_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.std)
s <- ggplot(data=shan_ict_s_df, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_density(color="black",
               fill="light blue") +
  ggtitle("Min-Max Standardisation")

shan_ict_z_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.z)
z <- ggplot(data=shan_ict_z_df, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_density(color="black",
               fill="light blue") +
  ggtitle("Z-score Standardisation")

ggarrange(r, s, z,
          ncol = 3,
          nrow = 1)

The course asks what statistical conclusion the histograms support. The three panels have the same shape and differ only in the numbers on the x axis. Both methods are linear transformations, so they change the location and scale of a variable but not its skewness or the relative positions of the townships. Standardisation evens out the weight of each variable in the distance calculation, and it does not make a skewed variable normal.

Computing the proximity matrix

dist() supports six distance measures, euclidean, maximum, manhattan, canberra, binary and minkowski, with euclidean as the default. I computed the euclidean distance between every pair of townships.

Show the code 
proxmat <- dist(shan_ict, method = 'euclidean')
Show the code 
proxmat

The printed matrix has 1,485 distances, one for each pair of the 55 townships, so I left it out of the rendered page.

WarningThe distances use the unstandardised values

The notes standardise the variables and then build proxmat from shan_ict, the raw rates. I followed the notes so that the results stay comparable, but I checked how much each variable contributes.

Show the code 
round(sapply(shan_ict, var) / sum(sapply(shan_ict, var)), 3)
   RADIO_PR       TV_PR  LLPHONE_PR   MPHONE_PR COMPUTER_PR 
      0.160       0.366       0.024       0.444       0.006

MPHONE_PR and TV_PR together account for 81 percent of the total variance, and COMPUTER_PR for less than 1 percent. In the raw scale the clusters are mostly built from mobile phones and television. I come back to this at the end of Part 3.

Computing hierarchical clustering

hclust() supports eight agglomeration methods, ward.D, ward.D2, single, complete, average (UPGMA), mcquitty (WPGMA), median (WPGMC) and centroid (UPGMC). Following the notes, I used ward.D.

Show the code 
hclust_ward <- hclust(proxmat, method = 'ward.D')
Show the code 
plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6)

The tree has one very tall final merge at a height of about 4,336, which joins a group of 31 townships with a group of 24. Below that, the next merges happen at 1,820 and 1,443.

Selecting the optimal clustering algorithm

agnes() from cluster works like hclust() but also returns the agglomerative coefficient. It measures how strong the clustering structure is, and values closer to 1 mean a stronger structure. I computed it for four methods.

Show the code 
m <- c( "average", "single", "complete", "ward")
names(m) <- c( "average", "single", "complete", "ward")

ac <- function(x) {
  agnes(shan_ict, method = x)$ac
}

map_dbl(m, ac)
  average    single  complete      ward 
0.8131144 0.6628705 0.8950702 0.9427730

Ward’s method has the highest coefficient at 0.943, ahead of complete linkage at 0.895, average at 0.813 and single linkage at 0.663. Single linkage chains townships one at a time, which gives the weakest structure. I use Ward’s method from here on.

Determining the optimal number of clusters

The notes list three common methods for choosing the number of clusters, the elbow method, the average silhouette method and the gap statistic, and use the gap statistic.

Gap statistic method

The gap statistic compares the within cluster variation for each k with the value expected from data with no cluster structure. The best k is the one with the largest gap. clusGap() from cluster computes it, and hcut() from factoextra does the hierarchical clustering inside each run.

Show the code 
set.seed(12345)
gap_stat <- clusGap(shan_ict, 
                    FUN = hcut, 
                    nstart = 25, 
                    K.max = 10, 
                    B = 50)
# Print the result
print(gap_stat, method = "firstmax")
Clustering Gap statistic ["clusGap"] from call:
clusGap(x = shan_ict, FUNcluster = hcut, K.max = 10, B = 50, nstart = 25)
B=50 simulated reference sets, k = 1..10; spaceH0="scaledPCA"
 --> Number of clusters (method 'firstmax'): 1
          logW   E.logW       gap     SE.sim
 [1,] 8.407129 8.680794 0.2736651 0.04460994
 [2,] 8.130029 8.350712 0.2206824 0.03880130
 [3,] 7.992265 8.202550 0.2102844 0.03362652
 [4,] 7.862224 8.080655 0.2184311 0.03784781
 [5,] 7.756461 7.978022 0.2215615 0.03897071
 [6,] 7.665594 7.887777 0.2221833 0.03973087
 [7,] 7.590919 7.806333 0.2154145 0.04054939
 [8,] 7.526680 7.731619 0.2049390 0.04198644
 [9,] 7.458024 7.660795 0.2027705 0.04421874
[10,] 7.377412 7.593858 0.2164465 0.04540947
Show the code 
fviz_gap_stat(gap_stat)

The largest gap is at k = 1 (0.274), so the statistic suggests the townships form one group. That is not useful for segmentation. Among k from 2 to 10, the largest gap is at k = 6 (0.2222), which is why the notes choose six clusters.

The choice of six is weak. The gap at k = 5 is 0.2216 and at k = 4 is 0.2184, both within 0.004 of k = 6, while the standard error for each is about 0.04. Any k from 4 to 6 fits the data about equally well. I keep six so that the rest of the results can be compared with the notes.

The notes also mention NbClust, which reports 30 indices for the number of clusters and proposes the best scheme across combinations of distance measures and clustering methods. The exercise does not run it.

Interpreting the dendrogram

Each leaf of the dendrogram is one township. Similar townships are joined into branches lower down, and the height of a fusion shows how different the two groups are. Two townships can only be compared by the height at which their branches first join. Their positions along the horizontal axis say nothing about similarity.

rect.hclust() draws boxes around the six clusters. The notes give border = 2:5, which has only four colours, so two clusters would reuse colours. I gave it six.

Show the code 
plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6)
rect.hclust(hclust_ward, 
            k = 6, 
            border = 2:7)

Visually driven hierarchical clustering

heatmaply combines the dendrogram with a heatmap of the variables, so the reason each township sits in its cluster can be read off the colours.

Transforming the data frame into a matrix

heatmaply() expects a matrix, so I converted the data frame first.

Show the code 
shan_ict_mat <- data.matrix(shan_ict)

Plotting an interactive cluster heatmap

Show the code 
heatmaply(normalize(shan_ict_mat),
          Colv=NA,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D",
          seriate = "OLO",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 6,
          margins = c(NA,200,60,NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main="Geographic Segmentation of Shan State by ICT indicators",
          xlab = "ICT Indicators",
          ylab = "Townships of Shan State"
          )

Hovering over a cell shows the township, the variable and its min-max value. This heatmap clusters the normalised values, so its six groups are not exactly the same as the ones from hclust_ward, which used the raw values. The darkest block, high on television, mobile phones and computers at once, holds the border trade towns Muse, Tachileik, Laukkaing and Mongla together with Taunggyi, Lashio, Kengtung and Pangsang.

Mapping the clusters

I cut the tree into six clusters with cutree().

Show the code 
groups <- as.factor(cutree(hclust_ward, k=6))

groups is a factor with one label per township. To map it, I converted it to a matrix, attached it to shan_sf with cbind() and renamed the new column to CLUSTER.

Show the code 
shan_sf_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER`=`as.matrix.groups.`)
Show the code 
qtm(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER")
Show the code 
table(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)

 1  2  3  4  5  6 
20  4 13  6  7  5

The clusters are very fragmented. I counted the number of separate pieces each cluster forms on the map, using the contiguity neighbour list from Part 4.

Show the code 
nb_check <- poly2nb(shan_sf)

count_pieces <- function(cl) {
  sapply(sort(unique(cl)), function(g) {
    suppressWarnings(n.comp.nb(subset(nb_check, cl == g)))$nc
  })
}

count_pieces(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)
1 2 3 4 5 6 
4 4 5 5 5 1

Five of the six clusters are split into four or five separate pieces. Only cluster 6 is one connected block, Mongmao, Pangsang, Hopang, Pangwaun and Mongyang in the Wa area along the Chinese border. This is the main limitation of a non-spatial method. Townships end up together because their ICT profiles match, whether or not they are anywhere near each other.

A check, clustering the standardised variables

Since the raw scale gives MPHONE_PR and TV_PR most of the weight, I reran the same Ward clustering on the min-max values to see how much the grouping depends on that choice.

Show the code 
groups_std <- cutree(hclust(dist(shan_ict.std), method = "ward.D"), k = 6)

table(raw = groups, standardised = groups_std)
   standardised
raw  1  2  3  4  5  6
  1 14  1  4  0  0  1
  2  0  1  0  0  3  0
  3  0  6  5  2  0  0
  4  0  0  0  5  0  1
  5  1  0  0  0  4  2
  6  0  0  0  1  0  4

The two solutions agree only in part. Cluster 1 from the raw values mostly stays together, but cluster 3 splits three ways and townships from cluster 5 spread across three groups. With the variables on equal terms, radio and land line phones get more say, and several townships change neighbours in the tree. The rest of this page follows the notes and uses the raw values.

ImportantMy takeaway

Ward’s method gave the strongest structure, and the gap statistic pointed to six clusters only by a very small margin over four or five. The six clusters make sense in ICT terms, with a border town group high on almost everything and a Wa group with very little radio. On the map they are scattered across Shan State. I also learned that leaving the variables unscaled hands most of the decision to mobile phones and television.

Part 4, Spatially constrained clustering with SKATER

SKATER (Spatial ’K’luster Analysis by Tree Edge Removal) only allows neighbouring townships to join the same cluster. It links all townships in a minimum spanning tree, where each link is between two neighbours, and then cuts the tree into pieces. Each piece is one cluster and is contiguous by construction.

Converting to SpatialPolygonsDataFrame

The notes convert shan_sf into an sp object because older versions of the SKATER functions only accepted sp.

Show the code 
shan_sp <- as_Spatial(shan_sf)
Notesf works directly now

Current versions of spdep accept sf objects in poly2nb(). I ran poly2nb() on both shan_sf and shan_sp and got identical neighbour lists, so the conversion is no longer needed. I kept it to follow the notes.

Computing the neighbour list

Show the code 
shan.nb <- poly2nb(shan_sp)
summary(shan.nb)
Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 55 
Number of nonzero links: 264 
Percentage nonzero weights: 8.727273 
Average number of links: 4.8 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 
 5  9  7 21  4  3  5  1 
5 least connected regions:
3 5 7 9 47 with 2 links
1 most connected region:
8 with 9 links

The 55 townships have 264 neighbour links, an average of 4.8 each. Five townships have only two neighbours, regions 3, 5, 7, 9 and 47, which are Ywangan, Mabein, Pekon, Nawnghkio and Pangwaun. Region 8, Lawksawk, has the most with nine.

I plotted the network on top of the township boundaries. The boundaries go first, since the first plot sets the extent and the network would otherwise clip parts of the map. The centroids of the polygons serve as the nodes.

Show the code 
coords <- st_coordinates(
  st_centroid(st_geometry(shan_sf)))

plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), 
     border=grey(.5))
plot(shan.nb,
     coords, 
     col="blue", 
     add=TRUE)

Computing the minimum spanning tree

Calculating edge costs

nbcosts() gives each neighbour link a cost, the euclidean distance between the two townships in the five ICT variables. A low cost means two neighbours have similar profiles.

Show the code 
lcosts <- nbcosts(shan.nb, shan_ict)

I then turned the neighbour list into a weights object with these costs as the weights. Style "B" keeps the costs as they are, without row standardisation.

Show the code 
shan.w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, 
                   lcosts, 
                   style="B")
summary(shan.w)
Characteristics of weights list object:
Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 55 
Number of nonzero links: 264 
Percentage nonzero weights: 8.727273 
Average number of links: 4.8 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 
 5  9  7 21  4  3  5  1 
5 least connected regions:
3 5 7 9 47 with 2 links
1 most connected region:
8 with 9 links

Weights style: B 
Weights constants summary:
   n   nn       S0       S1        S2
B 55 3025 76267.65 58260785 522016004

S0, the sum of all weights, is 76,268. Each link appears twice in the list, once in each direction, so this is twice the total cost of the 132 links.

Building the minimum spanning tree

mstree() finds the set of 54 links that connects all 55 townships with the lowest total cost.

Show the code 
set.seed(1234)
shan.mst <- mstree(shan.w)
Show the code 
class(shan.mst)
[1] "mst"    "matrix"
Show the code 
dim(shan.mst)
[1] 54  3

The tree has 54 rows, one fewer than the number of townships, since a spanning tree on n nodes always has n minus 1 edges. Each row holds the two townships at the ends of an edge and its cost.

Show the code 
head(shan.mst)
     [,1] [,2]      [,3]
[1,]   28   12  78.78999
[2,]   12   49  59.69478
[3,]   28   13  92.79567
[4,]   13   52 110.55197
[5,]   49   35 124.74445
[6,]   35   37  91.65458
NoteThe first rows differ from the notes

My first rows do not match the notes, which start with townships 54 and 48. mstree() picks a random starting township when ini is not given, and the order of the rows follows the order in which the tree grows. I built the tree from two different seeds and got exactly the same 54 edges with the same total cost of 9,686.6 both times. Only the order changes, and SKATER gives the same clusters as the notes. I added set.seed() so the output above stays the same on every render.

Show the code 
plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), 
                 border=gray(.5))
plot.mst(shan.mst, 
         coords, 
         col="blue", 
         cex.lab=0.7, 
         cex.circles=0.005, 
         add=TRUE)

Compared with the neighbour network, each township now has only the links needed to keep the tree connected, and there are no loops.

Computing spatially constrained clusters

skater() takes the two node columns of the tree, the data used to update the costs as groups form, and the number of cuts. Six clusters need five cuts.

Show the code 
clust6 <- spdep::skater(edges = shan.mst[,1:2], 
                 data = shan_ict, 
                 method = "euclidean", 
                 ncuts = 5)
Show the code 
str(clust6)

groups holds the cluster label of each township. edges.groups describes each cluster with its nodes, edges and within cluster sum of squares (ssw). ssto is the total sum of squares, and ssw at the top level records the criterion after each cut.

Show the code 
ccs6 <- clust6$groups
ccs6
 [1] 3 3 6 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 2 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 2 4 1 2 5 1 1 1 2 1 2 2 1 2 2 1 1 3 1 2
[39] 2 2 2 2 2 4 1 3 2 1 1 1 2 1 2 1 1
Show the code 
table(ccs6)
ccs6
 1  2  3  4  5  6 
22 18 11  2  1  1

The six clusters have 22, 18, 11, 2, 1 and 1 townships. The notes say the first cluster has 12 nodes, but the node vector of the first element of edges.groups has length 22, matching the table.

Show the code 
round(clust6$ssw)
[1] 12613 10977  9962  9540  9123  8735

The first cut does most of the work. It lowers the criterion from 12,613 to 10,977, and each later cut takes off only between about 390 and 1,020. The last three cuts remove small branches, which is why cluster 4 has two townships and clusters 5 and 6 one each.

Show the code 
shan_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(SP_CLUSTER = ccs6) %>%
  filter(SP_CLUSTER %in% 4:6) %>%
  select(SP_CLUSTER, TS.x, RADIO_PR, TV_PR, LLPHONE_PR, MPHONE_PR, COMPUTER_PR) %>%
  arrange(SP_CLUSTER)
  SP_CLUSTER    TS.x  RADIO_PR    TV_PR LLPHONE_PR MPHONE_PR COMPUTER_PR
1          4 Mongpan 228.74008 517.2477   21.58273  437.7421   46.485888
2          4 Langkho 227.46781 587.1483   74.39199  403.9103   32.308059
3          5 Narphan  75.27012 210.0886   42.18769  305.2689    3.277892
4          6 Ywangan 484.52147 260.5734   11.93591  120.2856    4.414650

The singletons are extreme townships. Ywangan has the highest radio rate in the state and the sixth lowest television rate. Narphan has the lowest computer rate in the state and the third lowest television rate. The tree can only isolate them by cutting them off, since every possible region around them would contain townships unlike them.

I plotted the pruned tree on the map. The notes give five colours for six groups, so I added a sixth.

Show the code 
plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), 
     border=gray(.5))
plot(clust6, 
     coords, 
     cex.lab=.7,
     groups.colors=c("red","green","blue", "brown", "pink", "orange"),
     cex.circles=0.005, 
     add=TRUE)

Visualising the SKATER clusters

Show the code 
groups_mat <- as.matrix(clust6$groups)
shan_sf_spatialcluster <- cbind(shan_sf_cluster, as.factor(groups_mat)) %>%
  rename(`SP_CLUSTER`=`as.factor.groups_mat.`)
qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER")

For comparison I put the hierarchical clusters and the SKATER clusters side by side.

Show the code 
hclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_cluster,
                  "CLUSTER") + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

shclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster,
                   "SP_CLUSTER") + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

tmap_arrange(hclust.map, shclust.map,
             asp=NA, ncol=2)

Every SKATER cluster is one connected region. Cluster 1 covers the central and southern belt from Hsipaw down through Loilen to Monghsat. Cluster 2 runs along the whole eastern border from Muse and Lashio to Tachileik and Kengtung. Cluster 3 is the western edge from Mongmit down to Pinlaung, including Taunggyi.

Show the code 
shan_sf_spatialcluster %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(SP_CLUSTER) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_RADIO_PR = mean(RADIO_PR),
            mean_TV_PR = mean(TV_PR),
            mean_LLPHONE_PR = mean(LLPHONE_PR),
            mean_MPHONE_PR = mean(MPHONE_PR),
            mean_COMPUTER_PR = mean(COMPUTER_PR))

4 4              2         228.        552.            48.0           421.
5 5              1          75.3       210.            42.2           305.
6 6              1         485.        261.            11.9           120.
# ℹ 1 more variable: mean_COMPUTER_PR <dbl>

The three large regions have clear profiles. Among them, the eastern border region (cluster 2) has the highest land line, mobile phone and computer rates but the lowest radio rate, 174 per thousand. The western region (cluster 3) has the highest radio rate at 329 and fairly high television. The central belt (cluster 1) is lowest of the three on television, mobile phones and computers.

The price of contiguity shows in the spread within clusters. Cluster 2 joins the border towns of Muse and Tachileik with the Wa townships of Pangsang and Mongmao because they lie on the same border, even though hierarchical clustering put them in different groups. I measured the share of total variance explained by each solution with a small helper.

Show the code 
r_squared <- function(cl) {
  x <- as.matrix(shan_ict)
  tss <- sum(sweep(x, 2, colMeans(x))^2)
  wss <- sum(sapply(unique(cl), function(g) {
    xg <- x[cl == g, , drop = FALSE]
    sum(sweep(xg, 2, colMeans(xg))^2)
  }))
  1 - wss / tss
}

c(hclust = r_squared(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER),
  skater = r_squared(ccs6))
   hclust    skater 
0.7610272 0.4998530

The hierarchical clusters explain 76 percent of the variance in the five variables, and the SKATER clusters only 50 percent.

ImportantMy takeaway

SKATER turned the scattered pieces into three large connected regions, west, centre and eastern border, plus three tiny clusters for townships too unusual to fit anywhere. That contiguity cost a lot of homogeneity, with the explained variance falling from 76 to 50 percent. Asking for six clusters did not give six useful regions here, because three of the five cuts went into trimming outliers.

Part 5, Spatially constrained clustering with ClustGeo

ClustGeo offers a softer constraint. Its hclustgeo() function runs a Ward-like hierarchical clustering on two dissimilarity matrices at once. D0 holds the differences in the clustering variables and D1 holds the differences in space. A mixing parameter alpha between 0 and 1 sets the balance. At alpha = 0 only D0 counts, and at alpha = 1 only geography counts. The aim is to find an alpha that makes the clusters more compact on the map without losing too much homogeneity in the variables, and choicealpha() helps with that.

Ward-like hierarchical clustering with ClustGeo

With only D0, hclustgeo() is an ordinary Ward clustering. D0 has to be a dist object, so I reused proxmat.

Show the code 
nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, 
            k = 6, 
            border = 2:7)

Mapping the clusters

Show the code 
groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k=6))

shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)

qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER")

This map is close to the hclust() map from Part 3 but not the same.

Show the code 
table(hclustgeo = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER, 
      hclust_ward.D = shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)
         hclust_ward.D
hclustgeo  1  2  3  4  5  6
        1 16  0  0  0  0  0
        2  4  1  0  0  3  0
        3  0  0 13  0  0  0
        4  0  0  0  6  0  0
        5  0  3  0  0  4  0
        6  0  0  0  0  0  5

Clusters 3, 4 and 6 are identical, and eight townships move between clusters 1, 2 and 5.

Notehclustgeo() matches ward.D2

hclustgeo() applies Ward’s criterion to squared distances, which is what hclust() calls ward.D2. I ran hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D2") and got exactly the same six clusters as hclustgeo(proxmat). The difference above comes from Part 3 using ward.D. The agnes() coefficient of 0.943 also belongs to ward.D2, since agnes(method = "ward") gives the same tree as ward.D2.

Show the code 
count_pieces(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER)
1 2 3 4 5 6 
6 5 5 5 6 1

Without the spatial term these clusters are just as fragmented as before, with only cluster 6 in one piece.

Spatially constrained hierarchical clustering

D1 is the distance between townships. st_distance() returns a matrix of distances between polygons, and as.dist() turns it into a dist object.

Show the code 
dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)

st_distance() measures from boundary to boundary, so the 132 pairs of townships that share a border all have a distance of 0. The longest distance is about 444 km.

choicealpha() runs the clustering for alpha from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1 and reports how homogeneous the six clusters are in each space.

Show the code 
cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat, range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), K=6, graph = TRUE)
Show the code 
round(cbind(cr$Q, cr$Qnorm), 3)
             Q0    Q1 Q0norm Q1norm
alpha=0   0.757 0.131  1.000  0.139
alpha=0.1 0.740 0.284  0.978  0.301
alpha=0.2 0.647 0.626  0.855  0.665
alpha=0.3 0.624 0.692  0.825  0.735
alpha=0.4 0.527 0.831  0.697  0.882
alpha=0.5 0.493 0.874  0.652  0.928
alpha=0.6 0.493 0.874  0.652  0.928
alpha=0.7 0.480 0.879  0.635  0.934
alpha=0.8 0.411 0.940  0.543  0.999
alpha=0.9 0.375 0.918  0.496  0.975
alpha=1   0.191 0.941  0.252  1.000

Q0 measures homogeneity in the ICT variables and Q1 in space, and the normalised versions are scaled to 1 at their best. At alpha = 0, Q0 is 0.757 and Q1 only 0.131. Moving to alpha = 0.2 raises Q1 to 0.626 while Q0 falls to 0.647, or 85 percent of its maximum. Beyond 0.2 the trade gets worse. Alpha = 0.4 gains another 0.2 in normalised Q1 but loses 0.16 in normalised Q0. Following the notes, I use alpha = 0.2.

Show the code 
clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)
Show the code 
groups <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k=6))
Show the code 
shan_sf_Gcluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)
Show the code 
qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER")
Show the code 
table(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER)

 1  2  3  4  5  6 
10  9  7  9 12  8
Show the code 
count_pieces(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER)
1 2 3 4 5 6 
2 1 5 7 1 2

The six clusters are more balanced in size than SKATER’s, from 7 to 12 townships, and more compact than the non-spatial ones. Clusters 2 and 5 are fully connected, and clusters 1 and 6 form two pieces each. ClustGeo does not force contiguity, though. Cluster 3 still has five pieces and cluster 4 is spread over seven.

Show the code 
shan_sf_Gcluster %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(CLUSTER == "4") %>%
  pull(TS.x)
[1] "Mabein"    "Kyaukme"   "Muse"      "Lashio"    "Tachileik" "Laukkaing"
[7] "Hseni"     "Namhkan"   "Taunggyi"

Cluster 4 holds the main towns of the state, Taunggyi, Lashio, Kyaukme, Muse, Namhkan, Laukkaing, Tachileik, Hseni and Mabein. Their ICT profiles are so close to each other, and so far from the townships around them, that a spatial weight of 0.2 is not enough to split the group by location. For a planning map this group reads as an urban type, and it would need a separate treatment from the regions around it.

I put the four solutions side by side and compared how much variance each explains.

Show the code 
tmap_arrange(qtm(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER") + tm_title("hclust, ward.D"),
             qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER") + tm_title("ClustGeo, alpha = 0"),
             qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER") + tm_title("SKATER"),
             qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER") + tm_title("ClustGeo, alpha = 0.2"),
             ncol = 2)
Show the code 
tibble(method = c("hclust ward.D", "ClustGeo alpha = 0", "ClustGeo alpha = 0.2", "SKATER"),
       r_squared = c(r_squared(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER),
                     r_squared(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER),
                     r_squared(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER),
                     r_squared(shan_sf_spatialcluster$SP_CLUSTER)),
       pieces_on_map = c(sum(count_pieces(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)),
                         sum(count_pieces(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER)),
                         sum(count_pieces(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER)),
                         sum(count_pieces(shan_sf_spatialcluster$SP_CLUSTER)))) %>%
  mutate(r_squared = round(r_squared, 3))
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  method               r_squared pieces_on_map
  <chr>                    <dbl>         <dbl>
1 hclust ward.D            0.761            24
2 ClustGeo alpha = 0       0.757            28
3 ClustGeo alpha = 0.2     0.647            18
4 SKATER                   0.5               6

The two non-spatial solutions explain about 76 percent of the variance and break into 24 and 28 pieces on the map. ClustGeo with alpha = 0.2 explains 65 percent with 18 pieces, and SKATER explains 50 percent with exactly 6. ClustGeo sits between the two extremes, which is what the mixing parameter is for.

ImportantMy takeaway

ClustGeo gave me a dial between homogeneity and compactness, and choicealpha() made the trade visible. At alpha = 0.2 most regions became compact while keeping 85 percent of the homogeneity. It also showed something SKATER hides, a group of main towns spread across the state that are more like each other than like their neighbours.

Part 6, Visual interpretation of clusters

The notes profile the clusters from shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, the ClustGeo solution with alpha = 0, so I used the same object.

Visualising one clustering variable

Show the code 
ggplot(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster,
       aes(x = CLUSTER, y = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_boxplot()

Cluster 3 has the highest radio ownership, with a median of 278 households per thousand. Cluster 2 follows at 227 and cluster 1 at 205. Cluster 4 is lower at 155, and clusters 5 and 6 are lowest, both with a median of 97.

WarningThe ranking in the notes

The notes rank the clusters 3, 2, 1, 4, 6 and 5 by mean radio ownership. The means in the summary table at the end of the notes, which I reproduce below, give 3, 2, 1, 4, 5 and 6, with cluster 5 at 124 and cluster 6 at 98.6. The boxplot shows medians, and on medians clusters 5 and 6 are tied.

Multivariate visualisation

A parallel coordinate plot shows all five variables at once, with one line per township. ggparcoord() from GGally draws it, and facet_grid() gives each cluster its own panel. Columns 17 to 21 of shan_sf_ngeo_cluster are the five clustering variables.

Show the code 
ggparcoord(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, 
           columns = c(17:21), 
           scale = "globalminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of ICT Variables by Cluster") +
  facet_grid(~ CLUSTER) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))

Cluster 4 stands out with the highest television and mobile phone ownership, and it also leads on land lines and computers. These are the six border and trade towns, Muse, Tachileik, Laukkaing, Mongla, Namhkan and Taunggyi.

Cluster 5 has the lowest television, mobile phone and computer rates of all six clusters. The notes say it is lowest on all five items, but cluster 6 has less radio and cluster 2 has fewer land lines.

scale = "globalminmax" draws the raw values on one shared axis. ggparcoord() offers five other options. std subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, and robust subtracts the median and divides by the median absolute deviation. uniminmax rescales each variable to run from 0 to 1. center applies uniminmax and then centres each variable on a summary value set by scaleSummary, and centerObs does the same around one chosen observation set by centerObsID.

With globalminmax, television and mobile phones fill most of the height and computers are squashed along the bottom. I also drew the same plot with uniminmax, which puts every variable on the same 0 to 1 range.

Show the code 
ggparcoord(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, 
           columns = c(17:21), 
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plots of ICT Variables by Cluster, uniminmax scale") +
  facet_grid(~ CLUSTER) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))

On this scale the computer rate of cluster 4 becomes visible, and so does the land line profile of cluster 6, which sits fairly high even though its radio rate is the lowest. No scale is best for every purpose, and switching between them helped me read the clusters.

Summary statistics

I computed the mean of each clustering variable by cluster to back up the plots.

Show the code 
shan_sf_ngeo_cluster %>% 
  st_set_geometry(NULL) %>%
  group_by(CLUSTER) %>%
  summarise(mean_RADIO_PR = mean(RADIO_PR),
            mean_TV_PR = mean(TV_PR),
            mean_LLPHONE_PR = mean(LLPHONE_PR),
            mean_MPHONE_PR = mean(MPHONE_PR),
            mean_COMPUTER_PR = mean(COMPUTER_PR))
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  CLUSTER mean_RADIO_PR mean_TV_PR mean_LLPHONE_PR mean_MPHONE_PR
  <chr>           <dbl>      <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>
1 1               221.        521.            44.2           246.
2 2               237.        402.            23.9           134.
3 3               300.        611.            52.2           392.
4 4               196.        744.            99.0           651.
5 5               124.        224.            38.0           132.
6 6                98.6       499.            74.5           468.
# ℹ 1 more variable: mean_COMPUTER_PR <dbl>

The six clusters can be read as six ICT profiles. Cluster 4 is the connected urban group, with 744 televisions and 651 mobile phones per thousand households and a computer rate of 65.5. Cluster 3 has the most radios (300) and fairly high television (611). Cluster 6, the Wa townships, has the fewest radios (98.6) but relatively high land line and mobile phone ownership. Cluster 5 is the least connected group, with 224 televisions, 132 mobile phones and 6.7 computers per thousand. Clusters 1 and 2 sit in between, with cluster 2 especially low on land lines (23.9).

Wrapping up

The five ICT rates group Shan State’s 55 townships into six profiles that range from a connected urban group to a group with very low ownership of every item. Without a spatial constraint these profiles are scattered across the state in 24 to 28 separate pieces. SKATER produced three connected regions, west, centre and eastern border, plus three outlier clusters, at the cost of explaining only 50 percent of the variance. ClustGeo with alpha = 0.2 kept 65 percent, made most clusters compact, and left the main towns together as one scattered urban group.
